nodes.name: AI design patterns to avoid
nodes.html:
The habits an agent repeats when it decides alone. Each one, on its own, looks like a choice; together they are the signature of "a page made by AI". Applies to landing pages, sites, apps and any visual piece.

Read before choosing a direction and again when reviewing the first version.

PatternWhy avoid itInstead
Purple or blue gradientThe number one marker of a generated pageColor taken from the project's real reference (brief question 1). Gradient only if the reference calls for it, and never purple to blue
Default typeSerif italic became every AI's shortcut for "elegant"; Inter, Space Grotesk, Plus Jakarta Sans, DM Sans and Roboto are its shortcut for "clean"A face chosen for a reason that comes from the reference: a sans with character, a display face, condensed, or hand-lettering. Write the reason down
Grid background (squares, dots, lines)Filler to hide emptiness; on almost every "tech" templateTexture, photo, flat color or deliberate empty space
3 generic benefit cardsIcon + title + two lines, three times, side by side: the most copied block on the webThe benefit inside proof (photo, number, before/after), an asymmetric list, one big benefit and the rest smaller
Emoji in the copyCheapens the text and gives away generated copyNone. If a visual marker is needed, use an icon from the page's own system
Glow on everything (text, buttons, borders)Everything glowing means nothing stands outContrast of color and size. If there's an effect, on one element only
The usual layoutCentered hero → 3 cards → testimonials → FAQ → CTA: the spine of every AI pageNo need to reinvent the wheel every time, but break at least the order or the composition: asymmetric hero, a section that bleeds into the next, a rhythm of different sizes
Generic iconsThin-line Lucide/Feather are the invisible defaultAn icon drawn for the project, a cut-out photo, or less-used families (Phosphor, Solar) with a chosen weight
Everything staticA still page looks like a mockup, not a productMotion with a purpose: scroll entrances, hover that responds, one live element in the hero. Respect prefers-reduced-motion
01 / 02 / 03 on an unordered listThe number suggests a sequence. On loose items (services, benefits) it's decoration that implies steps that don't existNumber only when order matters (steps, stages, timeline). Loose lists go without numbers
Hard shadows and boxes everywhere (neo-brutalism)Offset shadows with no blur, thick black outlines, square corners on every block, buttons that "press" into their shadow. The agent's escape from the purple gradient; it reads as a tool whatever the business isEdges and depth by role and by the reference's material: a border or shadow only on the one element that must stand apart, a radius that matches the real objects, shadow only where the light is real
Spec-sheet dressingMonospace in nav, buttons and labels; lot numbers, temperatures, coordinates, barcodes, "status: live" bars, countdowns nobody asked forOnly the data the visitor acts on (hours, price, pickup), in the page's own text face. Mono only for real code or tables
A default AI lookThe second set of defaults: warm cream + terracotta (often with a serif), near-black + one acid-green or vermilion pop, the newspaper broadsheet, receipts/tickets/stamps as the conceptThe look comes from the brief's own object and feeling. Any of these only when brief question 1 named it, and never in more than one of the three directions

Plus the niche list from : the look everyone in this niche already repeats.

Running from generic is not the goal

An agent that avoids every tell and every niche cliché can make a page that no longer looks like the business (grey cement and mono labels for a barbershop, a technical spec sheet for a bakery). Keep what visitors of the niche expect; originality goes on top of it.

  • 3-second test: would a customer of this niche know what the business is, and want it, from the first screen alone?
  • Fit test: do the edges, shadows, lines, texture, type and motion match the feeling from the brief? (references/visual-language.md in the off-template skill.)

How to check

Run the list on full-page screenshots of the finished page (desktop and 390 px) and on its source, never on the first screen alone; and on each mockup. Write down each item: absent, present, or present on purpose (with the reason from the brief). Three or more present means the page still looks AI-made: go back to the brief, don't just swap colors. Either fit test failing sends the direction back too.

See also: · ·

nodes.name: Design brief
nodes.html:
Without a chosen aesthetic direction, the agent decides on its own, and its default is the same for everyone. Clean, and generic. The brief is the only defense against shipping the same page with swapped colors to the fifth client in a row.

The 4 questions

Ask the person. Never answer these yourself unless they say so in words ("you decide"). A one-line prompt is not that.

  1. What place or object in the real world represents this brand? The palette comes from here, not from a nice-looking hex.
  2. What should a visitor feel in the first 3 seconds? One feeling. If there are two, nothing has been chosen yet.
  3. Two unexpected influences to combine. The collision is what makes something that didn't exist before.
  4. What must this page never look like? The most useful of the four, and the one nobody asks.

Always offer 3 or 4 concrete options with each question, so answering is a click. If the person doesn't understand a question, don't rephrase it: give new options. Example for question 1, burger place: "a griddle at 2 a.m.", "a 70s diner counter", "a butcher's paper wrap", "a neon sign in the rain".

The options steer the answer. Question 1 mixes kinds of reference (the place, the product, a person or gesture, a moment), with at most one printed-paper object (bag, label, receipt, stamp, newspaper), and one option is what the niche's own customers would name first. Question 2 offers feelings, not styles.

Before the direction of a demo or a spec site, also pin down who pays for it: size of the business, ticket, neighborhood, clientele. The concept has to fit them.

Anti-convergence rules

These work across projects, not inside one:

  • No hex from memory. Color comes from question 1, every time. A good way: find a photo of the real object (Wikimedia Commons works), sample its pixels, then check text contrast before committing.
  • Don't repeat a style. Read every note in 20 Projects/ first. Colors and fonts can come back; the whole combination (reference + emotion + collision) can't. Controlling only color and font, over time, leaves you with only odd colors.
  • The collision has to show. If the two influences of question 3 aren't visible on the page, there was no collision.
  • One wildcard element. Something that doesn't fit perfectly, and that's why it sticks in memory (a slider the visitor drags, a portrait breaking out of its band, a ribbon of color through the title).
  • Name the vibe. 2 to 4 words. An aesthetic without a name turns generic the moment you execute it.
  • Run the anti-patterns () before closing a direction.

The equation behind every decision

Conversion = Desire - (Effort + Confusion)

Raise desire with specifics. Cut effort with brevity. Cut confusion with clarity. Every design decision serves one of the three; if it doesn't, it's decoration.

Where the effort goes

Half on the first screen. It's where the page is won or lost, and the only part every visitor sees.

---

The vibe discovery, the anti-convergence rules and the equation come from 2389-research/landing-page-design (MIT), rewritten and trimmed.

See also: · ·

nodes.name: Design rules
nodes.html:
Every rule in force for creating, reviewing or auditing a site, page or UI, one per line. Read in step 1 of . The story behind each rule lives in and .

Process

  • No step of the checklist can be skipped, even with a detailed request. If one can't be done, say which and why.
  • Before code: the 4 questions of the , the research (), the 3 directions as gray skeletons and one colored mockup per direction, both before asking for the choice. The mockup isn't optional and doesn't become a question.
  • Every direction defines its motion (what moves and why); a page with nothing moving doesn't ship. Ask the person for a motion reference (an app, site or video) and the intensity at the brief.
  • Every direction writes its visual language (edges, depth, lines, surface, type voice, motion feel), each with a reason from the reference; the build doesn't add a shadow, border or radius that isn't there.
  • Avoiding clichés is not the goal: direction A is one a customer of the niche recognizes in 3 seconds, and the three directions differ in visual language, not only in color.
  • Mark the direction you recommend, with the reason, when showing the three.
  • A showcase, docs page or your own project's site is a site: full checklist, with logo and favicon in the direction.
  • Before the direction of a demo, define who pays for the site (size, ticket, neighborhood, clientele) and make the concept fit them.
  • A report the person attaches applies in full, including the visual part, not only the list of sections.
  • Before delivering, run on the screenshot of the finished page and say which items still show up.

Visual and media

  • A portrait in the hero goes cut out, without background, never inside a rounded card with a shifted color block behind it.
  • Generated photo: first check that the niche's objects are right, then light and composition. All photos of a project share one base scene written at the start of every prompt.
  • The materials fit the feeling: a warm, hand-made business never gets hard offset shadows, black outlines and mono labels by default.
  • Horizontal scroll: test with mobile emulation on, every page, at 375/768/1024 px. A wide display title is sized by its column (cqi), so one long word can't overflow.
  • Multi-page SEO: title, description, canonical and Open Graph image per page (never in the shared layout), plus sitemap and robots.
  • WebGL or shader background: only with a real GPU, DPR 1, start on idle, and run Lighthouse mobile before delivering.
  • Slow continuous CSS motion: enable only after confirming GPU acceleration; test in Chrome with --disable-gpu.
  • Animated component: position on a wrapper and animation on the inner element, inherited text color, hidden items with display:none; check on a dark background and with reduced motion.

Forms

  • Every field gets real handling, not just a placeholder: phone mask, date with type="date" (no past dates for bookings), numbers that refuse letters on typing and paste, maxLength on text, counter on textareas, long text that wraps (overflow-wrap:anywhere).
  • When fixing one field, review every field on the site and test the worst case: pasting long text without spaces, typing letters in a number.
  • The same limits are validated on the server, not only in the field.
  • A checklist, filter or choice made before a WhatsApp or email button has to be in the message that gets sent.

Patterns that worked

From what the person praised (). New praise: entry in Wins and the pattern in one line here.

  • Let the visitor handle the product's number-one argument on the first screen, instead of only showing it (the view slider).
  • Take the identity from the business's physical objects and lock one base scene for every photo (home-style restaurant).
  • Show each direction as a gray skeleton plus one colored mockup before asking for the choice (barbershop).
  • A client with their own identity in posts: sample palette, letterforms and tone from them and bring the most recognizable element to the first screen (personal trainer).
  • An animated background from a reference: rebuild it in the brand colour and make it light the page's elements; lower intensity on phones (off-template site).

nodes.name: Research real sites
nodes.html:
Before drawing directions, look at what already exists. The research tells you two different things, and mixing them up is the trap:

  • what visitors expect to find (keep it: missing it costs trust);
  • what everyone in the niche looks like (avoid it: copying it makes you generic, just generic for the niche).

1. Collect 8 to 15 sites

Sources, in this order: links the person sent; web search for the niche plus the city or country ("burger restaurant website", "best burger restaurant websites", award galleries like Awwwards or Land-book filtered by the niche); the competitors the person names. Mix ordinary local sites with the best ones you can find: you need both the norm and the ceiling.

Open each one in a browser you can drive and screenshot the first screen at desktop and 390 px. Screenshots stay local: never commit third-party screenshots to a public repo.

2. Note the same things for every site

FieldWhat to write
Section orderHero → menu → about → ...
Hero layoutCentered text over photo, split, full-bleed video, product cutout...
PaletteMain colors in words and hex (sampled from the screenshot)
FontsFamily or style (condensed sans, script, slab, mono)
ImageryProduct photo, people, illustration, stock, user photos
MotionNone, scroll reveals, video, hover effects
Main CTAText and where it sits
TierGeneric, solid, premium, outlier

3. Turn it into two lists

Keep (what visitors expect). What 70% or more of the sites have and a visitor would miss: for a burger place, menu with prices, address and map, hours, order/delivery button, photos of the actual food.

Avoid (the niche's sameness). The look most of them share: e.g. black background with red and yellow, grunge textures, a script font for "since 19xx", a dark hero photo with a burger and smoke. This becomes a niche-specific list of anti-patterns for this project, on top of the general ones.

Also write down: what separates premium from generic (usually photography quality, restraint in color, real typography, one strong idea) and the outliers (who breaks the rules and still works, and how).

4. How each direction uses the research

  • A, best of the niche: at the level of the premium sites, keeping everything in the keep list and none of the avoid list.
  • B, break the convention: take the strongest item of the avoid list and do the opposite on purpose.
  • C, outside reference: bring in a world from outside the niche (the brief's two unexpected influences) while keeping the keep list.

Each skeleton says which finding it came from ("B: every site is black and red, so B is daylight cream with one ketchup red").

5. Save it

Vault: 10 Notes/Styles of <niche>.md, linked from , so the next project in the same niche starts from it. No vault: design/research.md in the project.

When sites won't open

Some sites will fail (blocked network, certificate errors). List which ones and keep going with the rest. If fewer than 8 opened, say so and ask the person for links at STOP 1. Don't fill the gap with guesses or with second-hand articles presented as if you had seen the sites.

Rules

  • Extract patterns, never copy images, copy or logos from another site.
  • No search or browser available at all: ask the person for 5+ links, or for screenshots, and analyze those.

See also: · ·

nodes.name: Skeletons before code
nodes.html:
Before the first line of code, show style options as wireframes, the way a designer would in Figma, and build only after the person picks one. This holds even when the request already lists palette, fonts and sections.

Each direction has

  • A named vibe (2 to 4 words) and one sentence on why, including which research finding it came from.
  • The first screen at 390 px and at desktop, in gray blocks: a box with an X where a photo goes, lines where text goes, a rectangle for each button.
  • The whole page's section order, as small labeled blocks.
  • 3 or 4 color swatches and the font names. The only color on the skeleton.
  • The wildcard element marked with a label ("portrait cut out, breaking past the band", "slider: the view at each hour").
  • The logo and the favicon idea, in one line each.
  • The motion: what moves on this page and why (a live element in the hero, how sections enter, what responds to hover). One or two lines.

The three must differ in composition

Not just color. Change where the photo sits, the size of the title, the rhythm of the sections. If you can swap the palettes between two directions and they become the same, they're one direction.

Skeleton rules

  • Gray and white. The only color is the swatch strip, so the person judges composition without being distracted.
  • No lorem ipsum. Real title and button text, or close to it.
  • Run on each before showing.

Where to build them

  • Claude Code: one Artifact with the three side by side (tabs or columns, each with a phone frame and a desktop frame). Private by default, opens on the phone by link, and updates in place after feedback.
  • Other agents: one local design/skeletons.html with the same layout, served locally; give the person the path or the local URL.

Before sending, look at the page at 390 px in a real browser (resize_window in Claude Code), not only at desktop, and reset the size afterward. Headless Chrome won't go below ~500 px wide, so its "390 px" screenshots are wrong unless you use device emulation.

Save a PNG screenshot of each direction in design/ too: it's what goes into the mockup prompts and the project history.

See also: · ·

nodes.name: Styles of burger food trucks
nodes.html:
Based on: 12 sites (6 US, 2 UK, 2 Australia, 2 Brazil), opened on 2026-10-26 for the burger example of the off-template repo (examples/burger-2026-10/off-template/research.md). Comes with the vault as an example of a niche note.

A fixed burger shop has the same menu and ordering, but swaps "where we are today" for a fixed address and hours. The Brazilian sample is thin: both sites were delivery-platform menus, not the trucks' own sites.

Keep: what almost all of them have

  • Where the truck is today, on the first screen: stop name, hours, a map link.
  • A weekly schedule with dates, easy to scan on a phone; an honest "closed for the season" when it is.
  • The menu with real prices, short enough to read at a glance.
  • A close photo of one burger: melted cheese, crust, pickles.
  • One clear order action ("Order online" or "Call") visible without scrolling.
  • Instagram, because that's where trucks post last-minute changes.
  • Trust facts in one line: halal, beef source, hours, payment.
  • A separate, quiet path for events and catering.

Typical section order

  1. Today's stop + the order action
  2. Menu with prices
  3. This week's schedule
  4. Photos / Instagram
  5. Catering
  6. Footer with hours and contacts

Avoid: the look everyone repeats

  • A hero with only a logo or a slogan, no food and no location.
  • The schedule hidden behind an external link or "see our Facebook".
  • A phone number as the only way to order.
  • The comic palette: red + yellow + black with Bangers or Anton in caps, and emoji.
  • Catering pages that read like a marketplace, with dozens of SEO town links.
  • Mixing a fixed shop and a truck without saying which is open today.
  • Content that only loads by script: an empty page for search and slow phones.
  • Template wording ("Taste Extraordinary Now") instead of the name, the street and the price.

What separates premium from generic

  • Premium is a well-shot burger and a schedule you can read in two seconds.
  • Generic is the template with a slogan and a mascot.

Outliers worth knowing

  • Smash Up (Annapolis): today's stop is the first thing on the page, above the logo's tagline. It answers the only question a truck visitor has.
  • IronMikes: a plain "closed for the season, back in spring" banner. Honest beats empty.

See also: · ·

nodes.name: Halfway
nodes.html:
Style: Fisheye Session

A burger cut in half, shot like a frame of a skate video through a fisheye lens in front of the truck at night. The first 3 seconds feel loud and a little crooked, like a friend saying "you have to try this". The collision: skate video × butcher shop (white butcher paper wrap, plain proud copy). The wildcard: the round photo drifts with the pointer like a handheld camera.

Palette: #3c2828 char · #7e321b edge char · #e9ab68 cheese (only the order button) · #dcbc9d bun crumb · Fonts: Bowlby One / Karla

Direction file: examples/burger-2026-10/off-template/direction.md in the off-template repo.

Comes with the vault as an example. A new burger site reading this note must not repeat this style: another reference, another palette, other faces.

See also: · ·

nodes.name: Off-Template site
nodes.html:
Style: Darkroom Develop

The editor at night meets a photographer's darkroom: a page develops in a tray under a red safelight, from gray skeleton to colored mockup to finished page, which is the skill's own flow. A red beam of light comes down from above and lights the letters it touches. The wildcard: an agent window with three prompts; picking one rebuilds the rest of the page in that look, growing from the click as a circle with a liquid rim.

Palette: #141818 night · #1c2120 tray · #E5231B safelight red (the only accent) · #f4f4f4 headline · #acb0bc text · Fonts: Familjen Grotesk / Commit Mono

Direction file: design/direction.md in the off-template repo. Live at https://off-template-skills.vercel.app

Comes with the vault as an example.

nodes.name: Agent rules
nodes.html:
The only required read in the vault, together with . Every rule in force is here, one per line, grouped by subject. The story behind each one (what happened, wrong → right) lives in and , which are for lookup only.

Area rules (design, sales...) live in the area's rules note, not here. Keep this file short: the optional hook injects it into every session and has a size limit.

Every session

  • Before the first action: read and this file. Then only the notes of the task's area.
  • When the conversation gets summarized (context compacted, "continuing from a previous conversation"), re-read this file before the next action: the summary keeps what was done, not the rules.
  • Not sure about the path or the content: stop and say what's missing.
  • Open request for examples or options: list the ideas and let the person choose before building.
  • Before building, discover the skills, MCP servers and plugins available (); discovery is the truth, the note is an old snapshot.
  • Before using a tool that has a section in , follow its rules (e.g. say the cost before generating).
  • Check the docs before claiming how a tool or library works, especially when the person will build on top of it.
  • When writing down a path, say in which environment it was seen; before following a noted path, check it on the current machine.
  • An MCP server that doesn't show up: test it (process, tool list, one read call) before declaring it unavailable.
  • Never skip a step of a checklist in silence: say which one and why.
  • Answer in this order: Understood → What I read → Action → Result → Single question (only if blocked).

Thinking differently

  • Never decide an aesthetic alone: brief, research, 3 directions, the person chooses.
  • The person answers the brief questions. A one-line prompt is not permission to answer them yourself; only "you decide" in words is.
  • The vault's rules apply to you too, including on your own project's pages (showcase, docs). Read them as rules, not as material.
  • Don't grade your own work alone: show it to the person before publishing any score or quality claim.
  • No color hex from memory: color comes from a real-world reference or the client's own material.
  • Don't repeat a whole style (reference + feeling + collision) across projects: read 20 Projects/ first.
  • Research separates what visitors expect (keep) from what everyone repeats (avoid). Never copy the niche's look.
  • Prefer a ready piece (library component, skill, MCP tool) over a hand-made one; check its license.
  • A finished page is not done until the anti-patterns ran on its screenshot.

Logging (when fixing, not at the end of the session)

  • Non-trivial mistake: full entry at the end of and the rule in one line here, in its section. Test: would a future agent, without this conversation, fall into it again?
  • Rule that only applies to one area: goes to that area's rules note (design: ), not here.
  • Praise from the person: entry in and the pattern in one line under "Patterns that worked" in the area's rules note.
  • Idea for later: .

Git

  • Messages in English with added:, updated:, fixed: or deleted:.
  • Before the first commit, reuse the identity of the last commit.
  • Diagnose with a read-only command before anything that rewrites history or deletes files.
  • Local and remote diverged: merge, never force-push.

Vault

  • Folders: 00 Inbox/, 10 Notes/, 20 Projects/, 90 System/. Don't create others; no loose notes at the root besides indexes.
  • Links as [[Note name]]. Renamed a note: fix its links.
  • Never delete content without confirmation: archive to 00 Inbox/archive-YYYY-MM-DD.md.
  • A note read every session (INDEX, this file) stays short: one line per rule. Details and history go to lookup notes.

nodes.name: Capabilities
nodes.html:
What the agent has at hand: skills, MCP servers and plugins.

Rule

Before building anything, find out what you already have. Half of what an agent builds by hand already exists as a skill, an MCP tool or a library component (shadcn, React Bits). Checking costs one call; rebuilding costs the session.

Order:

  1. Run the discovery below. It's the source of truth.
  2. A skill or MCP exists for the job: use it.
  3. Nothing exists: then build by hand.
  4. What was missing was installable: log it in with the exact name.

Any list of tools written in a note is a snapshot, not the truth. It ages every session. Never decide "I don't have X" from a note.

How to discover

Claude Code

WhatHow
SkillsThe skill list in the system prompt; ListSkills if available
MCP servers/mcp, or claude mcp list in a terminal
Deferred MCP toolsToolSearch with a keyword: many tools only show their name until loaded
Plugins/plugin, or ListPlugins
Skills on disk~/.claude/skills/, <repo>/.claude/skills/, ~/.claude/plugins/

Other agents

AgentMCP configInstructions
Cursor~/.cursor/mcp.json, .cursor/mcp.json.cursor/rules/
Codex CLI~/.codex/config.tomlAGENTS.md
Copilot (VS Code).vscode/mcp.json.github/copilot-instructions.md

Skills are not a market standard: they're a folder with a SKILL.md. Any agent that can read files can read one and follow it by hand.

Installing

  • Skill: npx skills add <github-repo> (add --agent <name> for non-Claude agents), or copy the folder to ~/.claude/skills/<name>/. To write a new skill, use the skill-creator skill.
  • MCP server (connector): in the client's settings or MCP config. The connection is the person's (usually OAuth). Never paste tokens or keys into this vault, and never ask the person for them.
  • Plugin (Claude Code only): /plugin marketplace add <repo>, then /plugin install <name>.

Always ask the person before installing.

Snapshot

Write here what you found in the last discovery, with the date and the machine. It's only a reminder: run the discovery again anyway.

nodes.name: Mistakes
nodes.html:
Append only. The history behind the rules in and . Nobody reads this in full: the one-line rule is what matters, so always add it where it will be read.

The entries below come with the vault: real mistakes from the projects the off-template skill was built on, already turned into rules. Keep them, or delete them once you have your own.

Template

## YYYY-MM-DD: short title
- **What happened:** ...
- **Why it was wrong:** ...
- **Rule from now on:** (imperative, one line)
- **Wrong → right:** ...
- **Line added to:** Agent rules > (section), or Design rules

2026-09-28: answered the brief questions myself

  • What happened: the prompt was one line ("a site for a home-style restaurant"). The agent filled in the reference, the feeling and the influences itself and went straight to directions.
  • Why it was wrong: the brief is where the person's taste enters. Answered by the agent, it produces the agent's default page with extra steps.
  • Rule from now on: ask the 4 brief questions every time; only answer them yourself when the person says "you decide" in words.
  • Wrong → right: "I imagined a cozy rustic feel" → "Which real place or object should this feel like? a) the counter order pad b) grandma's kitchen c) a roadside diner d) other"
  • Line added to: Agent rules > Thinking differently

2026-09-28: a phone field that was only a placeholder

  • What happened: the contact form had placeholder="(11) 99999-9999" and nothing else. Letters, 40 digits and pasted paragraphs all went through to the WhatsApp message.
  • Why it was wrong: a placeholder shows the format, it doesn't enforce it. The message the business received was broken.
  • Rule from now on: every field gets real handling (mask, maxLength, counter, type), and the same limits on the server.
  • Wrong → right: a bare <input placeholder> → a masked phone field that refuses letters on typing and paste
  • Line added to: Design rules > Forms

2026-10-01: ran so far from generic that the site got ugly

  • What happened: to avoid the barbershop clichés, the direction took a cold, technical look with mono labels and hard shadows. Customers of the niche didn't recognize it as a barbershop.
  • Why it was wrong: avoiding clichés is not the goal. The page has to look like the business and make people want it.
  • Rule from now on: direction A is one a customer of the niche recognizes in 3 seconds; the other two take the risks.
  • Wrong → right: "a barbershop that looks like a spec sheet" → "the best barbershop site in town, then two bolder options"
  • Line added to: Design rules > Process

2026-10-02: showed only the gray skeletons

  • What happened: the three directions went out as gray skeletons; the colored mockups were offered as "optional, if you want".
  • Why it was wrong: nobody chooses a look from gray boxes. The person picked blind and asked for changes after the build.
  • Rule from now on: skeletons and one colored mockup per direction go out together, before asking for the choice.
  • Wrong → right: "here are 3 skeletons, want mockups too?" → "here are 3 skeletons and their mockups; I recommend B because…"
  • Line added to: Design rules > Process

2026-10-15: "no sideways scroll on phones" that wasn't true

  • What happened: the check ran in a narrow desktop window. On a real phone emulation one long word in the display title pushed the page sideways.
  • Why it was wrong: a narrow window is not a phone: no touch, no mobile viewport rules.
  • Rule from now on: test sideways scroll with mobile emulation at 375, 768 and 1024 px, every page; size wide titles by their column (cqi).
  • Wrong → right: "checked at 390 px, fine" → "checked with mobile emulation at 375/768/1024, every page, no sideways scroll"
  • Line added to: Design rules > Visual and media

2026-10-16: a shader background that froze machines without a GPU

  • What happened: a WebGL hero ran at full resolution from the first frame. On an office PC without GPU acceleration the page stuttered and scrolling froze.
  • Why it was wrong: the visitor's machine is not the developer's machine.
  • Rule from now on: WebGL only with a real GPU, DPR 1, started on idle and paused off-screen; run Lighthouse mobile before delivering.
  • Wrong → right: a shader on load at DPR 2 → a still frame first, the shader on idle, off when hidden
  • Line added to: Design rules > Visual and media

2026-10-20: delivered sites with almost no motion

  • What happened: two pages shipped with only a hover color change. They read as static templates.
  • Why it was wrong: a page with nothing moving is one of the AI tells. Motion has to be planned per direction, not added at the end.
  • Rule from now on: every direction defines its motion (what moves and why); ask for a motion reference at the brief.
  • Wrong → right: "added a fade-in" → "the photo rolls in once, the title settles, the buttons press; all off with reduced motion"
  • Line added to: Design rules > Process

2026-10-22: said "it's published" before publishing

  • What happened: the agent rebuilt the prototype and told the person it was live. The link still served the old version.
  • Why it was wrong: the person shared a link that didn't have the change.
  • Rule from now on: only say "live" after publishing and reloading the published version; before that, say "rebuilt, not published yet".
  • Wrong → right: "updated, check the link" → "published and reloaded: the link shows the new hero"
  • Line added to: Agent rules > Every session

nodes.name: Tool usage
nodes.html:
Rules per tool: cost, limits, gotchas. Each tool gets a section. Read the section before using the tool. Add a section the first time you use a new paid or media tool.

Which tool for which media

Fill in with your own choices. Starting point:

MediaTool
Gray skeletonsClaude Artifact (or a local HTML file)
Colored mockups, photos for the pageAn image model good at legible text (ChatGPT image generation, a GPT-image model through an MCP)
Video made from HTML (page scrolling, title card)HyperFrames
Animation on the siteGSAP (skills by GreenSock)

The full list of jobs and alternatives is in skills/off-template/references/tool-slots.md in the off-template repo.

Any credit-based tool

Always say how much a generation will cost before generating.

  1. Estimate the cost (most tools have a cost or simulate call).
  2. Read the current balance.
  3. Say: "This will cost X credits out of Y (Z left)." For a batch, the total and the per item.

Why: the credits belong to the person and don't come back. They decide if it's worth it, and they can only decide knowing the price.

Image models for mockups

  • Describe in the prompt what every item is. Models take a loose word literally ("Anatomy" turned into a human body).
  • They invent sample content (names, ratings, logos that look like real brands): give the exact text and say "nothing else".
  • Check the niche objects first (the right grill, chair, tool), then light and composition.

HyperFrames

Turns HTML + CSS + GSAP into MP4, frame by frame. Open source by HeyGen, free. It doesn't generate images or footage: it animates what's in the HTML.

  • Telemetry is on by default: npx hyperframes telemetry disable.
  • Before rendering: npx hyperframes lint and npx hyperframes snapshot --at 1,3.
  • Render needs FFmpeg; without it, render --docker (large image, slow the first time).
  • Google Fonts without @font-face fall back to another font in the render: embed the .woff2.
  • GSAP timeline with paused: true, registered in window.__timelines["<id>"].

Context7

Up-to-date library docs inside the agent. Use before claiming how a library works and when looking for shadcn or React Bits components. Check the free tier's monthly call limit and prefer one good query over several loose ones.

nodes.name: Wins
nodes.html:
Append only. What the person praised, so it becomes a pattern instead of luck. Each entry also goes, in one line, under "Patterns that worked" in (or the area's rules note).

The entries below come with the vault, from the projects the off-template skill was built on. Keep them, or delete them once you have your own.

Template

## YYYY-MM-DD: short title
- **Project:** ...
- **What was praised:** (the person's words, if possible)
- **Why it worked:** ...
- **Pattern:** (one line, reusable in other projects)

2026-09-23: a slider that shows the view at each hour

  • Project: an apartment launch facing a park
  • What was praised: "this is the thing people will play with"
  • Why it worked: the product's main argument (the view) became something the visitor moves in the hero, instead of a photo with a caption.
  • Pattern: find the product's number-one argument and let the visitor handle it on the first screen.

2026-09-28: the identity came from the restaurant's own objects

  • Project: a home-style restaurant
  • What was praised: "it looks like the place"
  • Why it worked: palette, type and texture came from the paper order pad, the enamel plates and the counter; every generated photo shared one base scene.
  • Pattern: take the identity from the business's physical objects and lock one base scene for every photo.

2026-10-01: gray skeleton plus a colored mockup per direction

  • Project: a barbershop
  • What was praised: "now I can choose"
  • Why it worked: the skeleton showed composition, the mockup showed the feel; together they made the choice easy and the build had no surprises.
  • Pattern: show composition (gray) and feel (one colored mockup) for each direction before asking for the choice.

2026-10-02: the look came from the client's own posts

  • Project: a personal trainer with a strong Instagram
  • What was praised: "it's me"
  • Why it worked: palette, letterforms and tone were sampled from the client's posts, and the most recognizable element went to the first screen.
  • Pattern: a client with their own identity in posts: sample it, don't invent a new one.

2026-10-26: a beam of light that lights the page

  • Project: the off-template showcase site
  • What was praised: the red light column in the hero
  • Why it worked: a reference the person loved (a light pillar effect) was rebuilt in an own shader, in the brand's red, and it lights the headline and the print as it passes instead of sitting behind them.
  • Pattern: an animated background from a reference: rebuild it in the brand colour and make it act on the page's elements; lower intensity on phones.
